claims.text: Laser preheating of the cutting zone will locally soften the Ti33Nb28Cr11V11Ni17 alloy.
Laser-induced local softening will reduce cutting forces relative to conventional machining.
Laser-assisted machining will reduce machining-induced work hardening relative to conventional machining.
Laser-assisted machining will reduce machining-induced grain refinement relative to conventional machining.
The starting material is a DED-fabricated Ti33Nb28Cr11V11Ni17 high-entropy alloy.
The alloy was produced from blended 45–150 μm, 99.9%-pure elemental powders on a Ti6Al4V substrate.
The starting alloy contains approximately 88.83% BCC A2 phase.
The starting alloy has an average grain size of approximately 3.66 μm.
The starting alloy has a microhardness of approximately 720 HV.
The starting alloy contains minor BCC B2 and Ti2Ni phases.
The proposed intervention uses laser preheating ahead of a TiAlN + SH-coated flat-end mill at 100 mm/min feed, 0.3 mm cutting depth, and 3 mm laser-to-tool separation.
The specified laser-assisted machining parameters will produce a surface temperature near 930 °C and a temperature of approximately 800 °C at 0.3 mm depth.
Approximately 800 °C lies within a softening regime of the alloy.
Transient laser heating reduces the local yield strength in the cutting zone.
Reduced local yield strength lowers cutting resistance, machining load, and vibration.
Reduced cutting resistance preserves a larger grain size after machining.
Laser-assisted machining will produce lower surface roughness than conventional machining.
Laser-assisted machining will cause a smaller machining-induced microhardness change than conventional machining.
Laser-assisted machining will not alter the alloy's chemical composition.
The alloy has an established high-temperature operational range of 22–1000 °C.
